title: Pointer arithmetic and arrays
lesson:
An array is a row of values side by side in memory. When you pass an array to a function, C doesn't copy it: it passes the address of the first item. We say the array **decays** to a pointer. That's why these two headers mean exactly the same thing:

```
int total(const int a[], int n);
int total(const int *a, int n);
```

**Pointer arithmetic.** If `p` points at an `int`, then `p + 1` points at the *next int*, not the next byte. C moves by the size of the type for you. So `a[i]` is just a shorter way to write `*(a + i)`.

```
int levels[4] = {50, 20, 70, 35};
int *p = levels;      /* points at levels[0] */
p++;                  /* now at levels[1] */
printf("%d\n", *p);   /* 20 */
```

**Walking with a pointer.** Instead of an index, you can move a pointer along the array and stop at the **end pointer**, which points one past the last item (allowed, as long as you never read it):

```
int sum = 0;
for (const int *q = levels; q < levels + 4; q++)
    sum += *q;
```

Many C libraries take a `start` and an `end` pointer like this, and so does C++'s whole standard library.

**Always pass the length.** Inside a function, the array is only a pointer, so it has no idea how long it is. `sizeof(a)` there gives the size of a *pointer* (4 or 8 bytes), not the array. This is the number one beginner bug with arrays in C. The habit: every function that takes an array also takes its length.

**const promises "I won't change it".** `const int *a` means the function may read the values but not write them. The compiler stops you if you try, and the caller knows their data is safe. Use `const` for every input array.

**Common mistakes:**
- Walking past the end: `q <= levels + 4` reads one item too many. Stop at `<` the end pointer.
- Using `sizeof` on a parameter to get the length.
- Mixing up `*p++` (read, then move the pointer) with `(*p)++` (add 1 to the value).

On a microcontroller, a serial buffer, an image's pixels or an audio sample block are all "a pointer and a length". Being fluent with them is what C is really about.

notes: average takes a start and an end pointer: it reads from start up to, but not including, end.
p++ moves to the next double, 8 bytes along, because C knows the type.
const double * means average promises not to change the readings.
show_size proves that inside a function an array is only a pointer: sizeof gives 8, not 40.
temps + 1 to temps + 4 is a slice of the array without copying anything.

exercises.title: Sum with a walking pointer
exercises.prompt: Write int sum_readings(const int *p, int n): the total of the n readings starting at p. Walk with the pointer itself (p++ or an end pointer); don't use square brackets anywhere in your code. With n of 0, return 0.

tests.name: only the first n
tests.hint_if_fail: Stop after n readings: const int *end = p + n;

tests.why: Walk with the pointer (*p, p++) instead of indexing with [ ].

hints: const int *end = p + n; marks the stopping point.
Or in one line: while (p < end) total += *p++;

exercises.title: Count in a range
exercises.prompt: Write int count_between(const double *start, const double *end, double lo, double hi): how many readings from start up to (not including) end are between lo and hi, inclusive. If start equals end there are no readings.

tests.name: part of the array
tests.hint_if_fail: Only look from start up to end, not the whole array.

hints: for (const double *p = start; p < end; p++)

exercises.title: Reverse in place
exercises.prompt: Write void reverse(int *a, int n) that reverses the n values in place (no second array), using two pointers that walk toward each other. n may be 0 (then a may be NULL).
hints: while (lo < hi) swap *lo and *hi, then lo++ and hi--.
Check n < 2 first and return: nothing to do.

quiz.q: p points at an int in an array. Where does p + 1 point?
quiz.why: Pointer arithmetic moves by the size of the type.

quiz.q: Inside void f(int a[]), what does sizeof(a) give?
quiz.why: The array decayed to a pointer, so pass the length separately.

choices: The function won't change the values a points to
The values are all the same
quiz.why: const before the type protects the data.

quiz.q: Walking with for (q = a; q <= a + n; q++) is...
choices: One step too far: it reads past the end
quiz.why: a + n is one past the end; stop with <.

quiz.q: Why do C libraries often take start and end pointers?
choices: A pair of pointers describes any slice of an array without copying it
Arrays can't be passed any other way
quiz.why: You can pass any piece of an array.

cards.q: Why always pass the length with an array?
cards.a: In a function, the array is just a pointer; it doesn't know its length.
Reads *p, then moves p to the next item.

cards.q: The end pointer of int a[n]?
cards.a: a + n: one past the last item, never read it.

explain: Explain in your own words why sizeof gives a different answer inside a function, with a small array example you make up.
